claims.text: A Pulumi blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' that covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS only and is AWS-centric (AWS-only, no multi-cloud support).
Multi-cloud is nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
AWS CDK, on which SST was originally built, lets developers define infrastructure using only TypeScript or Python.

With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code you write is not the code running during deployment.
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
Pulumi supports any programming language (the CTA card lists TypeScript, Python, Go, or C#).
Pulumi offers real-time debugging, whereas debugging AWS CDK is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK deployments because Pulumi uses direct execution while CDK is slower due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi offers cross-cloud secret support.
Pulumi extensibility includes custom providers and workflows.
Pulumi does not generate an intermediary format; it treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi Insights (product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features including custom providers and dynamic components.
With CDK/CloudFormation, the SST team often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve desired functionality.
SST's team migrated SST from CDK to Pulumi, re-implementing higher-level components built on CDK.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments documentation describes advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, and the AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi has an on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new SST deployment engine in which constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation, and once stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service, SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST is a framework for building modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST v3 keeps deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.
The SST team has repeatedly described SST's architecture as built on the Pulumi engine since the rewrite shipped.

The SST blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

The SST blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs page 'What is SST' says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."
Independent developers who compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi describe the same architecture of SST running on the Pulumi engine.

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi` plus first-party Pulumi providers (`@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`) and the Pulumiverse `@pulumiverse/vercel` provider as direct dependencies.
The SST repository is at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`).
In SST's deploy chain, the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and `sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components.
Terraform-bridged providers, via Pulumi's Terraform bridge, translate each Pulumi resource into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine handles dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and connectivity to hundreds of provider APIs for SST.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem with the Pulumi engine.
The Pulumi engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools in the same way, without requiring Pulumi-hosted services.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Embedding the Pulumi engine gives SST a production-grade provisioning engine and hundreds of cloud providers without building either from scratch.
Nitric, a cloud-agnostic application framework, runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine.
Nitric's docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang, which deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine.
The DefangLabs/pulumi-defang README describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
Nitric, Defang and SST expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Within an SST app, resources lacking a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly as raw Pulumi resources and deployed as part of the same app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode (anomalyco/opencode) has a larger GitHub star following than SST itself.
opencode has grown quickly since launch.
The team's work on opencode has not changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components use Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides centrally enforceable guardrails, and Pulumi components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be used with the same engine SST already runs on, without leaving it.
SST doesn't expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure sharing across multiple applications on its own.
SST is a strong fit for an opinionated full-stack application framework where infrastructure and code are defined together.
The linked post 'AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi' at /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ exists and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
The linked pages /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, and /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/ exist and cover the described topics.
